source: Every term the rooms and engines put on screen, in one plain sentence each, written for a reader who has never had a finance conversation. Lane 2, section 4 (DECISIONS.md L-4). The term list came from grepping rooms/*.html and engines/*.js for acronyms and capitalised phrases, plus the words a coaching client asks about.
confidenceNote: Definitions, not figures. Where a term has a legal meaning (a tax term, a plan name) the sentence says what it means for the reader, not the statute; the data tables carry the numbers and the sources.
note: Read by shared/glossary.js (SLAF.Glossary). `term` is the word as it appears on screen; `also` lists other spellings and the long form; `plain` is the sentence; `domain` groups them. No sentence uses its own term or any of its aliases (tests/glossary.test.js). Reading level: short sentences, common words, one idea each.

terms.plain: What lands in your account after tax and other deductions come out of your paycheque.
Everything you earn in a year before any tax or deduction is taken out.
What is left of a sum after the costs or taxes tied to it are taken away.
A plan for where each dollar of a month goes before the month starts.
Money coming in during a month set against money going out in the same month.
What is left at the end of a month when less went out than came in.
The gap when more goes out in a month than comes in.
The share of what you earn that you keep instead of spend, shown as a percent.
Cash set aside to pay for a surprise, like a car repair or a month without work, without borrowing.
How many months your cash would cover your spending if the money coming in stopped today.
Everything you own added up, minus everything you owe.
Anything you own that is worth money, like cash, a fund, a house or a car.
Money you owe to someone else, whatever it is called on the statement.
Money you have borrowed and still have to pay back, usually with interest.
How fast something you own can be turned into spendable cash without losing value or paying a penalty.
Something you own that takes months to sell, or costs a penalty to reach, like a house or a retirement account before 59 and a half.
Money in a checking or savings account that you can spend today.
Money put into something, like a fund or a business, that you expect to grow over time.
The part of a thing you truly own: its value minus any loan against it.
The amount originally borrowed or invested, before any interest is added.
The price of borrowing money, or the reward for lending it, paid as a percent of the balance.
The yearly cost of a loan as a percent of the balance, the number to compare loans by.
The yearly return on a savings account as a percent, with the compounding already counted.
Growth that earns growth: the return on last year's return is added to your balance too.
Growth counted only on the original amount, never on the earlier growth.
A percent applied to an amount, like the yearly percent charged on a loan or earned on savings.
The share of your whole income that actually goes to tax, all brackets averaged together.
The tax taken from the next dollar you earn, which is higher than the average on all your dollars.
A slice of income that is taxed at one percent; only the dollars inside that slice pay that percent.
The part of your income that tax is figured on, after the standard deduction and other subtractions.
A fixed amount everyone can subtract from income before tax is figured, no receipts needed.
An amount subtracted from income before tax is figured, so it lowers the tax bill by your bracket's share of it.
An amount subtracted from the tax bill itself, so a dollar of it saves a full dollar.
Tax your employer sends to the government from each paycheque on your behalf before you see the money.
A job where an employer pays you wages, takes out tax, and sends you the yearly form of that name.
Work paid without tax taken out, where you owe the tax yourself, named after the form the payer sends.
The Social Security and Medicare tax a person pays on their own business profit, both the worker's and the employer's halves.
The Social Security and Medicare tax taken from wages, about 7.65% for the worker with the employer matching it.
The government pension paid from age 62 on, sized by what you earned over your working years.
The government health insurance that starts at 65.
The most wages in a year that Social Security tax is charged on; above it, that tax stops.
The box on your tax return that says single, married together, married apart, or head of a household, which sets your brackets.
The filing status for a single person who pays most of the costs of a home for a child or dependant.
One tax return for a married couple, with brackets twice as wide as a single person's.
Two tax returns for a married couple, each on their own income, which usually costs more tax.
Your income after a few specific subtractions like retirement contributions, the figure many limits are based on.
Your income as the government counts it for a particular limit, with a few items added back; each rule has its own version.
The profit when you sell something for more than you paid for it.
Profit on something held more than a year before selling, which is taxed at lower rates than wages.
What you paid for something, the starting point for working out your profit when you sell.
When someone dies, what they paid for an asset is reset to its value that day, so the heir owes no tax on the earlier gain.
Cash a company or fund pays out to the people who own it, usually every few months.
The cash an investment pays each year as a percent of its price.
Growth measured after inflation is taken out, so it shows what the money can actually buy.
Growth measured in plain dollars, before inflation is taken out.
Prices rising over time, so the same dollar buys a little less each year.
The yearly growth a plan assumes for invested money, an assumption you can change, not a promise.
The share of a pot you can spend each year and expect it to last a lifetime, most often set at 4%.
A guideline that spending 4% of your investments in the first year, then adjusting for inflation, has lasted 30 years in the past.
Having enough invested that its growth can pay your bills, so work becomes a choice.
Saving hard enough to stop needing a paycheque years before the usual retirement age.
The pot you need so its growth covers your spending, usually 25 times a year of expenses.
The year your investments are projected to reach the pot that can pay your bills.
Having enough invested already that, with no more added, growth alone reaches the retirement pot by the usual age.
Working part time for health cover and some income while investments carry the rest.
Reaching independence on a smaller pot by planning to spend less than most people.
Reaching independence with a larger pot that supports more spending than most people.
The order good and bad years arrive in; bad years early in retirement hurt more than the same years later.
Keeping a few years of spending in cash and bonds so stocks are never sold in a bad year.
Slowly moving money from stocks to bonds as a goal gets closer.
The split of your investments between stocks, bonds and cash.
Which kind of account each investment sits in, chosen so the tax bill is smaller.
Owning just a US stock fund, an international stock fund and a bond fund.
A fund that owns every company in a list, like the 500 largest, instead of trying to pick winners.
A fund you buy and sell like a single stock during the day.
The yearly fee a fund takes, as a percent of what you hold in it.
An ordinary investing account with no tax break, no limit and no age rule on taking money out.
Money put into a retirement account before tax, so it lowers this year's tax bill and is taxed when taken out.
Money put into a retirement account after tax, so it grows and comes out later with no tax at all.
A retirement account you open yourself where contributions can lower this year's tax and withdrawals are taxed.
A retirement account you open yourself, paid with taxed money, whose growth is never taxed again.
A retirement account you open yourself, outside any job, with a yearly limit on what goes in.
A retirement account offered through a job, paid from your paycheque, often with money added by the employer.
The version of a workplace retirement account offered by schools, hospitals and non-profits.
A workplace retirement account for government workers that can be tapped after leaving the job at any age without penalty.
A retirement account for self-employed people that takes up to a fifth of business profit each year.
A small-business retirement plan with a lower yearly limit than a 401(k) and a required employer contribution.
A workplace-style retirement account for a business with no employees, where you contribute as both worker and employer.
Money your employer adds to your retirement account when you put some in, up to a stated share of your pay.
Earning the right to keep money or shares an employer gave you, which happens over a set number of years.
The timetable that says what share of an employer's grant is yours after each year.
A grant that is all yours on one date and none of it before.
Company shares promised to you that become yours on set dates and are taxed as wages when they do.
A workplace plan that lets you buy company shares from your paycheque at a discount.
The right to buy company shares later at a price fixed today, worth something only if the shares rise above it.
Put off until later: money or tax that is not due now but will be.
Extra money people 50 and over may add to a retirement account above the usual yearly limit.
The most the rules let you put into an account in one year.
An income range where a tax break shrinks bit by bit until it is gone at the top of the range.
Putting money into a traditional IRA and then moving it to the Roth kind, a route for people whose income is over the direct limit.
Adding after-tax money to a workplace plan above the usual limit and moving it into the Roth side.
Moving money from a pretax retirement account to the Roth kind and paying the tax on it now.
The amount the rules make you take out of a pretax retirement account each year from your seventies on.
A gift sent straight from a pretax retirement account to a charity after 70 and a half, which counts toward the yearly required withdrawal without being taxed.
An account you put money into for charity, getting the tax break now and choosing the charities later.
A savings account for medical costs that goes with a high-deductible health plan and is never taxed if used for care.
Health insurance where you pay more yourself before it starts paying, in return for a lower monthly price and the right to use a health savings account.
A workplace account for medical or childcare costs paid with untaxed money, most of which must be used within the year.
What you pay yourself on a claim before the insurance starts paying.
The most you can pay for covered care in a year; past it the plan pays everything.
The monthly or yearly price of keeping an insurance policy.
A fixed amount you pay at each visit or prescription.
Your share of a medical bill as a percent after the deductible is met.
Keeping your old job's health plan after leaving, for up to 18 months, paying the whole price yourself.
The government website where people without job coverage buy health insurance, with help paying based on income.
The mid-level marketplace plan whose price sets how much help everyone in the area gets.
Government help with the monthly price of marketplace insurance, larger when income is lower.
A yearly income figure the government publishes for each household size, used to set who qualifies for help.
The income line above which marketplace help disappears all at once instead of shrinking.
Free or very low-cost government health cover for people with low income.
Life insurance that pays a set amount if you die within a set number of years and nothing after.
Insurance that replaces part of your pay if illness or injury stops you working.
Extra liability cover on top of your car and home policies for a large claim against you.
A monthly charge added to a home loan when the down payment was under 20%, protecting the lender, not you.
The monthly fee a condo or neighbourhood charges every owner for shared upkeep.
Money collected with each mortgage payment and held to pay the property tax and home insurance when they come due.
The full monthly cost of a home loan: principal, interest, property tax and insurance together.
A loan to buy a home, paid back over many years, where the home is the lender's security.
Paying a loan off in equal payments where early ones are mostly interest and later ones mostly principal.
Replacing a loan with a new one, usually to get a lower rate or a different term.
What your home is worth minus what you still owe on it.
A line of credit you can draw on that uses your home as the security.
The loan as a percent of the home's value; 80% or lower avoids mortgage insurance.
Your monthly debt payments as a share of your monthly gross income; lenders like it under 36%.
A number from 300 to 850 that lenders use to guess how reliably you repay.
The record of your loans and cards, balances and payment history that the three credit bureaus keep.
Your card balances as a share of your card limits; under 30% helps your score.
Borrowing with no fixed end, like a credit card, where you can pay down and borrow again.
A loan with a fixed payment and a fixed end date, like a car loan or a mortgage.
The smallest amount a lender will accept each month without calling you late.
Paying extra on the debt with the highest rate first, which costs the least interest overall.
Paying extra on the smallest balance first for the quick wins, whatever its rate.
A low or zero rate on a card or loan that lasts a set number of months and then jumps.
Moving a card balance to another card with a low starting rate, usually for a fee of a few percent.
A federal student loan plan where the monthly payment is a share of your income rather than of the balance.
Federal student loans wiped out after 120 monthly payments while working for a government or non-profit employer.
The default federal student loan plan: the same payment every month for ten years.
The long-running federal plan that sets student loan payments at 10% or 15% of income above a living allowance.
A federal student loan plan from 2023 that courts blocked and Congress ended in 2026.
The federal student loan plan from July 2026 that charges 1% to 10% of income and forgives what is left after 30 years.
A pause on loan payments the lender agrees to, while interest keeps adding up.
A pause on federal student loan payments, during school or hardship, where the government may pay the interest for you.
The company that sends your student loan bills and handles your payments for the lender.
For student loan plans, your income above a set multiple of the poverty line; the payment is a share of this.
A lump sum an employer pays when they let you go, often a few weeks of pay per year worked.
Weekly money from the state while you look for work after losing a job, up to a cap and for a set number of weeks.
The year of past wages a state looks at to set your unemployment benefit.
A monthly payment for life from a past employer, sized by your years there and your pay.
A contract where you hand an insurer a lump sum and it pays you a set amount every month for life.
The monthly government pension the official website says you would get, at each starting age, based on your record so far.
The age, 66 to 67 depending on birth year, at which the government pension pays its full amount.
The 8% a year the government pension grows for each year you wait past full retirement age, until 70.
The monthly government pension you would get at full retirement age, the figure every earlier or later amount is scaled from.
The yearly raise to government pensions and tax limits that follows inflation.
Leave a job in or after the year you turn 55 and that job's retirement plan can be tapped without the early penalty.
The age after which retirement accounts can be tapped without the 10% early penalty.
A rule that lets you take fixed yearly amounts from a retirement account before 59 and a half without the penalty, if you keep it up for at least five years.
The extra 10% tax on money taken from a retirement account before 59 and a half, on top of ordinary tax.
A savings account for school and college costs whose growth is never taxed if spent on education.
The amount one person can give another in a year, $19,000 in 2026, without filing a gift tax form.
Everything a person owns and owes at the moment they die.
The person named on an account or policy to receive it when you die, ahead of anything a will says.
A label on an account that hands it straight to a named person at death, skipping the court process.
The court process that sorts out a dead person's property when no beneficiary or trust already says where it goes.
A signed document saying who gets what when you die and who looks after your children.
A legal container that holds property for someone, so it passes without the court process.
A document naming someone to handle your money or health decisions if you cannot.
The five families every number in this app belongs to: debt, assets, income, taxes, expenses.
The three needs that make up most of a month: food, accommodation, transportation.
The seven shares of take-home this app scores you on: debt, retirement, accommodation, food, transportation, taxes, therapy.
The Money Guy Show's nine steps for where each spare dollar goes, from a starter cushion to paying off the house.
The name of this suite of money rooms.
The family of small tools this app belongs to.
A well-known rule of thumb read against your own numbers, one card with a verdict and who it is for.
A what-if laid on top of your real numbers for a date range, like a house or a kid, that never changes the real numbers.
A saved set of choices in a room that you can come back to, kept beside your numbers rather than in them.
One of nine depths of detail in the ledger; going deeper sharpens the numbers, and nothing is ever locked.
The one place in this app where facts are typed in; every room reads from it.
How sure you are of a number: sure, roughly, or unknown, which decides how precisely it is shown.
The date a number was last true or last checked.
A number old enough that it should be checked again before it is trusted.
A dated copy of all your numbers kept so later change can be measured against it.
A number tried out to see what would happen, which is never saved as a fact.
One change you can make, like a raise saved or a cheaper home, sized in dollars a month and hours a week.
A bad turn added to a plan to see if it survives, like a market fall or months without pay.
A good turn added to a plan, like a raise you keep saving.
What a job pays per hour once commuting, unpaid overtime and work costs are counted against take-home.
The dollars a cheaper choice saves set against the hours of bother it costs, priced at your true hourly rate.
Which way an account is taxed: before you put money in, when you take it out, or never.
How reachable a pot is, from cash today to a home you would have to sell.
How often a number repeats: weekly, every two weeks, monthly or yearly.
A label from The Millionaire Next Door for someone whose net worth is at least twice their age times their income divided by ten.
How many dollars a single dollar invested at your age becomes by 65 at an assumed return.
The share of households your age with less than you, from the government's survey of finances.
The Federal Reserve's survey every three years of what American households own and owe.
The amount of cash that lets you stop worrying, chosen by you, not a formula.
What one bad year could cost you: the insurance deductibles and the months without pay, added up.
The share of household income that comes from one job or one person.
Borrowing at a rate above what investing would likely earn, so paying it off is the better return.
What the money could have earned somewhere else while it was doing this.
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's can be invested.
What an amount grows to by a later date at an assumed rate.
What a later amount is worth today, once the growth between now and then is taken out.
Investing a lump in equal slices over months instead of all at once.
Putting a whole amount in at once.
A large one-off amount that arrives, like an inheritance, a bonus or a payout.
Money or property you receive when someone dies.
A retirement account passed to you at someone's death, which most heirs must empty within ten years.
Living in one part of a property and renting out the rest so the rent covers most of the mortgage.
The number of years you would need to stay for buying to cost less than renting the same place.
A home's price divided by a year of rent for the same place; above 20 favours renting.
Everything a car costs a month: payment, fuel, insurance, upkeep and the value it loses.
The value a car or other thing loses each year just by getting older.
Owing more on a loan than the thing it bought is now worth.
The Money Guy Show's car rule: 20% down, a loan of no more than three years, and a payment under 8% of gross.
A budget where half of take-home goes to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to saving and paying down debt.
Ramit Sethi's approach: spend freely on the one or two things you love and cut hard on the rest.
A chart by the blogger Mr Money Mustache showing that your savings rate alone sets how many years until work is optional.
Bill Perkins's idea that money should be spent on experiences across life rather than left behind.
The book by Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez that prices every purchase in hours of your life.
Investors who follow John Bogle's advice: low-cost index funds, held for decades, with a simple mix.
A personal finance show by Brian Preston and Bo Hanson whose rules several lenses in this app use.
Scott Trench's book on saving half of take-home and house hacking, one of the sources for the DRAFTT bands.
The US government agency that collects federal tax and sets the yearly limits on retirement accounts.
The US government agency that runs the government pension and keeps your earnings record.
The US health department, which publishes the poverty guidelines each January.
The US labour department, which compiles each state's unemployment insurance rules.
A non-profit that publishes health insurance prices by state, including marketplace benchmarks.
A think tank that publishes every state's income tax brackets and property tax rates each year.
A number showing how expensive a place is compared with the US average set at 100.
The middle value: half of the group is above it and half below.
The share of a group that sits below a value; the 75th means three quarters are below.
The range a share is expected to sit in under a given rule, with under and over on either side.
One amount as a percent of another, like rent as a percent of take-home.
Turned into a yearly figure, like a monthly amount times twelve.
Working back from what you want to keep to the larger amount you would need before tax.
Pay that changes month to month, like freelance or commission work.
Tax that people without withholding pay in four instalments through the year to avoid a penalty.
Money set aside a little each month for a cost you know is coming, like a car or a holiday.
The lines you cannot skip for a month: food, a roof, getting around, and the bills tied to them.
Spending you choose rather than must do, from dinners out to subscriptions.
A bill that is the same every month and cannot be cut quickly, like rent or a loan payment.
The share of a month's spending you could drop within a month if you had to.
The lowest a month could cost if you kept only the fixed bills.
A month whose real totals have been entered, so its numbers stop being estimates.
What you planned to spend set beside what you really spent, the gap being the useful part.
Money you paid out that someone else will pay you back, so it is not really spending.
A child or relative who relies on your income and whom you can claim on your tax return.
